title: W-EDIT: A Wavelet-Based Frequency-Aware Framework for Text-Driven Image Editing
claim: One training-free mechanism handles many distinct editing operations, producing high-quality, structure-preserving results across diverse scenes and subjects.
layout: 4 stacked rows of 4 before/after pairs, dashed category boxes, captions below
description: A gallery of image-editing results arranged as four horizontal rows, each inside a rounded dashed-outline box with a gray label tab at the top left: Adding an object, Scene editing, Object replacement, and Non-rigid editing. Each row holds four examples. Every example is a single photo split down the middle, with the source image on the left and the edited image on the right. Below each pair is an italic quoted prompt fragment. Unchanged words are black. The new edit words are green. Replaced words are struck through in black. Examples include an astronaut gaining a flag, a lamp becoming a tree-branch lamp, a bicycle becoming a motorcycle, and a standing lion roaring. The eye goes first to the photos, which are saturated and photorealistic, and then to the green edit words.
caption: Representative editing results produced by W-Edit. Our training-free editing method is able to perform various types of image editing operations, including non-rigid editing, object addition, object removal, and global scene editing. These different edits are accomplished using the same mechanism.
abstract: While recent advances in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have significantly advanced text-to-image generation, text-driven image editing remains challenging. Existing approaches either struggle to balance structural preservation with flexible modifications or require costly fine-tuning of large models. To address this, We introduce W-Edit, a training-free framework for text-driven image editing based on wavelet-based frequency-aware feature decomposition. W-Edit employs wavelet transforms to decompose diffusion features into multi-scale frequency bands, disentangling structural anchors from editable details. A lightweight replacement module selectively injects these components into pretrained models, while an inversion-based frequency modulation strategy refines sampling trajectories using structural cues from attention features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that W-Edit achieves high-quality results across a wide range of editing scenarios, outperforming previous training-free approaches. Our method establishes frequency-based modulation as both a sound and efficient solution for controllable image editing.
